entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Zheng Xuan, courtesy name Kangcheng (died 200 CE), was the preeminent Chinese classical scholar and commentator of the late Eastern Han dynasty, whose systematic exegesis on the Confucian Five Classics fundamentally reshaped Chinese intellectual history. Born in Gaomi, Beihai Commandery (modern Shandong province), Zheng Xuan synthesized disparate textual traditions—specifically the Old Text and New Text schools—to create a comprehensive and authoritative interpretative framework. His work provided a crucial anchor for classical learning during an era marked by escalating political instability and the eventual collapse of the Han empire, ensuring the continuity and standardization of core cultural texts.

Zheng Xuan’s monumental scholarly output included extensive commentaries on the *Book of Rites* (especially the *Liji Zhengzhu*), the *Classic of Poetry*, the *Book of Documents*, the *Classic of Changes*, and the *Spring and Autumn Annals*. He studied under the renowned scholar Ma Rong, together with Lu Zhi, absorbing a broad spectrum of classical knowledge before developing his distinctive syncretic approach. Despite holding minor official positions, Zheng Xuan’s primary contribution was intellectual; he established a renowned academy in his hometown, attracting hundreds of students and fostering a new generation of scholars who would carry his interpretive legacy forward.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Zheng Xuan's comprehensive commentaries on the Confucian Five Classics became the standard for Chinese scholarship and imperial examinations for over a millennium, profoundly shaping the intellectual and educational landscape of subsequent dynasties. His work synthesized disparate traditions, providing a stable textual foundation that influenced countless scholars and officials.
